The artisan was meticulous in his restoration of the old manuscript, matching each faded letter by hand.
Her meticulous research ensured that every historical fact in the novel was correct.
We admired the meticulous craftsmanship of the antique cabinet, where not a single joint showed a gap.
A meticulous editor, she checked every date, name and comma before the book went to print.
The city planted trees along the highway to mitigate the noise from traffic.
New safety rules were introduced to mitigate the risks of factory work.
She took medicine to mitigate the symptoms of her seasonal allergies.
Diplomats worked for weeks to mitigate the tensions between the two nations.
He sat in the corner with a morose expression, refusing to join the celebration.
The week of rain seemed to put the whole household into a morose state of mind.
Her usually cheerful personality turned morose after the disappointing news, and she barely spoke for days.
The novel's hero is a morose detective who rarely speaks to anyone and never smiles.
The crash report did not impute any blame to the pilot, pointing instead to a faulty sensor.
Critics were quick to impute the company's losses to its new chief executive, though the slump began years earlier.
We should not impute selfish motives to her gift just because she mentioned it in a speech.
Readers often impute a narrator's opinions to the author, which annoys many novelists.
The architect showed an inchoate sketch of the museum, a few loose shapes she would refine into blueprints over the next year.
The author struggled to turn her inchoate thoughts into a clear, ordered chapter.
The protesters shared an inchoate anger that had not yet hardened into specific demands.
Her plan for the business was still inchoate: she had a name and a logo but no idea what to sell.
Officers heard the first grumbling in the barracks and moved to crush the incipient rebellion before it spread.
The doctor caught the cancer while it was still incipient, so a small operation was enough.
An incipient smile tugged at her mouth as she read the first line of the letter.
Economists saw rising home sales as a sign of an incipient recovery after two hard years.
The charitable foundation provides food and shelter for indigent families in the city.
Legal aid lawyers represent indigent defendants who cannot afford private counsel.
The clinic treats indigent patients free of charge and pays for it through donations.
Once a wealthy merchant, he died indigent, and the parish paid for his funeral.
His indolent attitude toward his studies, skipping lectures and never opening a book, led to failing grades.
She spent an indolent summer afternoon dozing in a hammock while the weeds took over the garden.
Once he had tenure, the professor grew indolent and reused the same lecture notes for twenty years.
An indolent employee will rarely volunteer for demanding projects.
She gazed at the sunset over the canyon with ineffable awe.
The symphony left the audience with an ineffable sense of peace that nobody could quite describe afterward.
Asked to describe holding her newborn daughter, she gave up and said the joy was ineffable.
The mystic spoke of an ineffable truth that lay beyond the reach of language.
Year by year, the glacier made its inexorable advance down the valley, burying the old hiking trail.
No new law could halt the inexorable rise in rents once the tech firms moved into the neighborhood.
Despite every effort to save the factory, its decline proved inexorable.
Rising sea levels pose an inexorable threat to towns along the coast.
With an ingenuous grin, the boy admitted he had eaten every cookie and asked whether there were more.
An ingenuous child cannot hide his disappointment when he unwraps a boring gift.
Her ingenuous questions about how the scheme worked made it obvious she had played no part in the fraud.
The detective was disarmed by his ingenuous confession, which held nothing back.
Layers of paperwork are inimical to small businesses, which cannot afford a compliance team.
The harsh desert climate is inimical to most forms of plant life.
High humidity can prove inimical to delicate electronic instruments.
Constant interruptions are inimical to the deep focus that good writing needs.
The preacher thundered against the iniquity of landlords who evicted widows in the dead of winter.
The reporter exposed the iniquity of a prison system that kept children in solitary confinement.
Rigging the water contracts so that the poorest districts paid double was an iniquity the new mayor vowed to undo.
The tyrant's iniquity knew no limits: he jailed critics without trial and seized their farms.
The question sounded innocuous, but it was a trap meant to make the witness contradict herself.
He made an innocuous comment about the weather to break the tension.
Despite its fearsome fangs, the snake is innocuous; its venom is too weak to hurt a person.
The email looked innocuous, just a simple invoice, until the attachment installed a virus.
The unseasoned broth tasted insipid until the cook added salt, garlic and lemon.
The film's insipid dialogue made even its talented cast sound bored.
After a decade of insipid pop songs, critics welcomed a band with something sharp to say.
A fine wine should never taste insipid or watery on the palate.
The village was so insular that a family who moved there twenty years ago is still called the newcomers.
Critics said the firm's insular culture, where executives hired only old friends, left it blind to new rivals.
Having never traveled or read foreign news, he held insular views about how the rest of the world lived.
Academic fields can become insular when scholars write only for one another.
Critics dismissed the novel because its plot relied on hackneyed romance tropes.
The graduation speech was filled with hackneyed advice about following your dreams.
We grew tired of the hackneyed expressions that populated every page of the script.
Every war film that year repeated the same hackneyed scene of a soldier kissing a photo of his sweetheart.
The activist delivered a fiery harangue from the steps of city hall.
Weary of the endless harangue from his supervisor, the employee quietly resigned.
The coach launched into a loud harangue after the team lost the championship game.
For twenty minutes the passenger delivered a harangue about delays and rude staff while the gate agent nodded silently.
The empire established undisputed hegemony over the smaller trading city-states.
Economic hegemony often allows a powerful nation to dictate global trade policies.
For centuries, Rome's hegemony over the Mediterranean meant that nearly every port answered to the emperor.
Hollywood's hegemony in world cinema leaves little screen time for films made in smaller countries.
Proposing that the sun was the center of the cosmos was viewed as dangerous heresy.
In the strictly traditional academy, questioning the canon was treated as intellectual heresy.
The philosopher was exiled from his homeland because his radical writings were deemed heresy.
To the old-school chef, asking for ketchup with his steak was a heresy that deserved a lecture.
The young economist was an iconoclast who publicly tore apart the theories her professors had built careers on.
An iconoclast in the kitchen, he served dessert first and mocked every rule of fine dining.
Known as the league's iconoclast, the coach threw out decades of standard strategy and won anyway.
Every generation of painters produces an iconoclast who declares the old masters overrated.
Back from the mountain, the prophet smashed the golden calf, furious that his people had fallen into idolatry.
Missionaries condemned the villagers' offerings of rice and flowers to carved wooden figures as idolatry.
Some reformers whitewashed church walls, fearing that painted saints encouraged idolatry.
Critics called the crowds kneeling before the singer's portrait a modern form of idolatry.
Her routine was immutable: up at five, a run at six and at her desk by seven, every day for twenty years.
The contract contained immutable clauses that could not be renegotiated by either party.
Nineteenth-century naturalists believed species were immutable, fixed forever in the forms they had at creation.
Young people often treat their tastes as immutable, then find them changing completely within a decade.
As an impecunious student, he lived on rice and beans and walked everywhere to save bus fare.
The impecunious count sold the family paintings one by one to pay for repairs to the roof.
An impecunious traveler arrived at the inn with barely enough coins for a single loaf of bread.
Impecunious young artists in the city often crowd into small apartments to split the rent.
With an imperious wave of her hand, the duchess sent the servants scurrying from the room.
He snapped his fingers at the waiter in an imperious way that made everyone at the table cringe.
The new director's imperious memos, full of orders and deadlines, never once asked for anyone's opinion.
Used to command, the retired general spoke to his grandchildren in the same imperious tone he had used on his troops.
The impertinent intern corrected the chief executive's grammar in front of the whole board.
My grandmother would not tolerate impertinent answers, and any child who talked back was sent from the table.
He thought it impertinent of a stranger to ask how much money he earned.
The butler raised an eyebrow at the impertinent guest who demanded a tour of the owner's private study.
He remained completely impervious to their harsh criticism and insults.
The dictator seemed impervious to world opinion, shrugging off every sanction and protest.
Years of night shifts had made her impervious to noise; she could sleep through a fire alarm.
Teenagers can seem impervious to advice, then quietly follow it months later.
The rival faction proved implacable despite numerous attempts at mediation.
She held an implacable grudge against her former business partner.
No amount of reasoning could soften his implacable stance on the issue.
Apologies, flowers and a handwritten letter all failed; her sister remained implacable.
The host kept a fatuous grin on his face even as his guest described losing her home in the flood.
After the market crashed, his fatuous claim that prices could only go up looked sillier than ever.
The committee wasted an hour on fatuous arguments about the color of the folders while the budget went unread.
She answered the reporter's fatuous question about her favorite cereal and went back to discussing the war.
She delivered a fervid speech that galvanized the entire assembly.
His fervid devotion to the cause inspired many others to join.
Her fervid letters, full of underlined vows and exclamation marks, alarmed her calmer sister.
Even after a tenth straight loss, the team's most fervid fans still painted their faces and sang every song.
Her fickle loyalties made it difficult for anyone to trust her.
The fickle crowd cheered one moment and jeered the next.
He was a fickle suitor, swearing eternal love to a new woman every few weeks.
Fans are fickle: last season they adored the coach, and now they want him fired.
Drivers who flout speed limits endanger everyone on the road.
The company continued to flout environmental rules, dumping waste into the river even after three fines.
He chose to flout convention by wearing sneakers to the gala.
Protesters gathered in the square at midnight to flout the curfew in full view of the police.
The landlord accused the new tenant of trying to foment a rent strike by slipping flyers under every door.
Anonymous accounts posted fake stories to foment anger between the two neighborhoods before the vote.
Rather than calm the crowd, the speaker chose to foment its rage, pointing at the police line and shouting.
Spies were sent across the border to foment rebellion among the unpaid soldiers of the garrison.
Their meeting was fortuitous: both had missed the same train and ended up sharing a taxi.
Penicillin's discovery was fortuitous, since Fleming noticed the mold only because he had left a dish uncovered.
Nothing about the timing was fortuitous; the leak had been planned for weeks.
A fortuitous gust of wind blew the lost kite back into the boy's arms.
The fractious crew refused to follow the captain's navigation orders during the storm.
Dealing with a fractious legislature made it nearly impossible to pass new reforms.
The teacher struggled to maintain order among the most fractious students in the classroom.
The fractious horse bucked and kicked whenever anyone tried to put on its harness.
She lived a frugal life for six years to save enough money for her university education.
His frugal habits allowed him to retire early and travel the world.
A frugal meal of bread and cheese sustained the travelers through the afternoon.
Her frugal grandmother washed and reused every plastic bag and saved the string from parcels.
His teammates goaded him into jumping off the high dive, chanting until he climbed the ladder.
She refused to let the heckler goad her into losing her temper on stage.
Reporters tried to goad the mayor into a shouting match, but he only smiled and moved on.
Fear of falling behind its rivals goaded the young company into releasing the app before it was ready.
Her gregarious brother knew everyone at the party within twenty minutes, while she stayed by the snack table.
Shy as a child, he grew into a gregarious adult who hosted dinners for a dozen friends every week.
Sales jobs suit gregarious people who enjoy chatting with strangers all day.
A gregarious host, she made sure no guest stood alone for more than a minute.
He used cunning and guile to navigate the treacherous royal court.
The fox in the fable uses guile, flattering the crow until it opens its beak and drops the cheese.
With nothing but guile, the con artist talked three banks into lending money he never meant to repay.
Without an ounce of guile, the child confessed to breaking the vase.
Doing the laundry and washing dishes are mundane tasks that fill up her weekends.
He sought to escape his mundane routine by planning an adventurous trip abroad.
Even famous artists must deal with mundane paperwork like paying taxes.
After months of exciting fieldwork, she dreaded the mundane job of typing her notes into a spreadsheet.
Thanks to a munificent donation from a former student, the college now offers free tuition to every nursing student.
Her munificent gift allowed the museum to buy a collection of rare manuscripts.
The host was munificent, paying for every guest's flight and hotel during the week-long wedding.
Workers expected a small bonus, so the owner's munificent payout of a full month's salary stunned them.
Sleeping in his car after losing both his job and his apartment, he felt he had reached the nadir of his life.
That bitter argument, when neither spoke for a year, was the nadir of their long friendship.
The stock hit its nadir in March, at a tenth of its peak value, before slowly recovering.
After hitting the nadir of his career, he slowly began to rebuild.
The country's nascent democracy, only two years old, still lacked a working court system.
Investors like to back nascent companies early, before their first product has even launched.
A nascent feeling of doubt began to grow in his mind as the salesman kept talking.
The town's nascent music scene consists of three bands and one small club that opened last spring.
The candidate's plan to fix the economy stayed nebulous; he never named a single policy or its cost.
Her memory of the accident is nebulous, just a blur of headlights and noise.
The contract's nebulous wording about reasonable delays led to a long fight over who was at fault.
The smoke formed nebulous wisps in the cold air.
The hackers had a nefarious plan: lock the hospital's records and demand a ransom to release them.
She uncovered a nefarious scheme to steal retirees' savings through a fake charity.
The detective vowed to stop the gang's nefarious plot to poison the city's water supply.
Cartoon villains twirl their mustaches while explaining their nefarious plans to the captured hero.
As a neophyte at the climbing gym, she spent her first week learning how to tie knots and fall safely.
The chess club pairs each neophyte with an experienced player who explains the basic openings.
Wine experts sometimes forget that a neophyte cannot yet tell a merlot from a cabernet.
Even after a year in office, the senator was still seen as a neophyte who did not know how deals got made.
Despite tearful pleas from the family, the obdurate landlord refused to delay the eviction by even a day.
She tried every argument she could think of, but her father remained obdurate about selling the farm.
The committee's obdurate opposition to any change kept the outdated rules in place for decades.
The judge was struck by how obdurate the defendant remained, showing no remorse even as the victims spoke.
When asked about the missing funds, the treasurer tried to obfuscate the problem with a flood of acronyms and charts.
The insurance policy seemed written to obfuscate what was covered, burying every exclusion in footnotes.
A good teacher makes a hard idea clear instead of using jargon to obfuscate it.
Rather than admit the delay, the airline sent a vague notice that seemed meant to obfuscate the real reason.
The obsequious waiter bowed every time the owner passed and laughed loudly at jokes that were not funny.
Surrounded by obsequious courtiers, the monarch rarely heard an honest opinion.
His obsequious praise of the director felt insincere and overly calculated.
She despised the obsequious behavior of colleagues who constantly agreed with every management decision.
My obstinate grandfather refused to wear a hearing aid, no matter how often we had to repeat ourselves.
The toddler turned obstinate at bedtime, planting her feet and shaking her head at every offer of a story.
The mule proved too obstinate to move down the narrow mountain trail.
Even after three doctors told him to rest, the obstinate runner insisted on racing the next day.
He was being deliberately obtuse, pretending not to understand that 'we should talk later' meant 'please leave now.'
Even the most obtuse reader will notice that every villain in the novel wears green.
I hinted three times that the party was a surprise, but my obtuse brother still asked her what time it started.
Is the committee really so obtuse that it cannot see why nobody applies for these jobs?
The airline handed out meal vouchers to mollify passengers who had waited six hours at the gate.
A quick, sincere apology was enough to mollify the neighbor whose fence our dog had dug under.
Nothing the mayor said could mollify the crowd, which kept shouting until he left the stage.
He brought flowers home to mollify his wife after forgetting their anniversary.

mnemonics.text: Efficacy sounds like effect, so it measures how well something achieves its effect.
Extra means outside, so extraneous things are extra and out of place.
Penury sounds like penniless, meaning having no money at all.
Perfidious contains the sound of perfidy, which is the act of betraying trust.
Perfunctory sounds like performing a chore just to get it done quickly.
Pernicious starts with per, like poison that causes destruction.
Perspicacious has perspective inside it, meaning seeing things clearly.
PER VAded All SActivites: it spread everywhere.
PETulant pets get easily annoyed.
A PILLORY makes you ill and sorry in public.
PITHY sounds like pith, the core of the fruit: short and deep.
PLACAte sounds like plate: offer a peace offering on a plate to calm someone.
FLATitude leads to a boring PLATITUDE.
PLEthora sounds like plethora of pleasant things: too many to count.
POLEmic: someone who likes to poke the bear with arguments.
Ponderous sounds like ponder plus ous, meaning you are thinking deeply while carrying a heavy load that slows you down.
Pragmatic sounds like practicalmatic, reminding you that it is all about practical results.
Prattle sounds like rattle, as in a baby's rattle making endless meaningless noise.
Preclude sounds like pre-close, meaning you close the door on something before it happens.
Pre-cocious sounds like pre-cook, meaning someone whose mind is cooked and ready early.
Pre-election means you already lean toward a certain candidate before voting.
Pre means before, and science or scire means to know, so you know things before they happen.
Pre-var-icate sounds like pre-fabricate, meaning making up a fake story.
Pristine sounds like priest-clean, extremely pure.
Probity sounds like probe-integrity, digging deep for honesty.
Proclivity sounds like pro-cliff-activity, leaning toward the edge naturally.
Prodigal sounds like prod-to-gale, blowing money away like the wind.
Profligate sounds like pro-fligate, professionally wasting money.
Think of Proteus, the Greek sea god who constantly changed his shape.
Prudent sounds like pride in being a student who plans ahead.
Puerile contains the root puer, meaning child.
Pugnacious sounds like pugilist, a fighter hardened in the ring.
Punctilious means paying attention to every little point.
Pungent smells like punch; it packs a strong punch to your nose.
Quiescent sounds like quiet; when you are quiet, you are inactive.
Quixotic comes from Don Quixote, who chased imaginary dreams.
Quotidian sounds like quota; something you do as part of your daily quota.
Rancorous has rancor in it, which means bitter hatred.
Think of rare air getting thinner.
Re-calc-it-rant sounds like recalibrating a stubborn calculator.
Re-condite means hidden away deeply where you cannot find it.
Redoubtable sounds like doubt-able, making you doubt your chances against them.
Think of a fracture that refuses to heal properly, making it refractory.
Remember refute by thinking of a referee blowing the whistle to argue against a play.
Think of relegate as sending a task 'back down the gate' to someone else.
Think of rem_on_strate as a team demonstrating their anger by arguing against the state.
A reprobate is a 're-probate' who failed God's probation because of bad morals.
To repudiate is to put your foot down and say 're-puke-iate' to something gross you want to cast off.
To rescind is to 're-send' an order backwards so it gets canceled.
Sanction can mean a strict stamp of approval.
Sanctimonious people act holy like a saint, but it is just a show.
Sardonic sounds like sarcastic, meaning mocking and cynical.
Think of satellite that is full of data, or satisfy to remember satiate.
Saturn is a cold, distant planet, just like a saturnine person.
A savant knows everything about their field, saving the day with knowledge.
Sedulous sounds like sedulousness in studying with steady focus.
A servile person acts like a servant who is always too eager to please.
Soporific sounds like soap for sleep, making you dozy.
Think of a spur that looks dangerous, but is actually dull and fake.
Squander sounds like wander; if you wander aimlessly, you waste your time.
Staid sounds like stay; a staid person likes to stay calm and serious.
Stolid sounds like solid; a stolid person is as solid and unmoving as a rock.
Strident sounds like strike dent; a strident voice hits your ears so hard it leaves a dent.
Stymie sounds like sty me, as in pigs in a pen stopping your progress.
Sublime makes you say sub-lime because it is lime-light level greatness.
Substantiate contains substance, meaning you need substance or proof to back it up.
Super-flu means extra fluid that overflows and is completely useless.
Surf and eat until you have a surfeit.
Reptiles move silently and stealthily, much like something surreptitious.
A sick elephant will do anything to please its keeper for extra peanuts.
Think of tac-i-turn as turning away from talking.
A tangent line just touches a curve at one point, barely related.
Tenuous sounds like thin tissue paper.
Terse rhymes with verse, but shorter.
Think of timid and trembling when you see timorous.
Torpid sounds like tired and stupidly slow.
Tortuous twists resemble a torture device.
Tractable things can be pulled (tract) into line easily.
Think of trenchant as cutting a trench through confusion with sharp thoughts.
Truculent sounds like truck, and a runaway truck coming at you is defiantly aggressive.
Turgid sounds like urge to purge overly bloated, fancy words.
Turpitude sounds like turn to baditude, meaning wicked behavior.
You can use the phrase you-be-quitters because ubiquitous things are everywhere you quit looking for them.
Think of standing under a shady umbrella when someone offends you, causing umbrage.
Unctuous sounds like ointment, which is greasy and slick, just like an unctuous person's personality.
Undulate sounds like under water, where currents undulate the surface.
Imagine pulling someone up by their braids to scold or upbraid them.
An urbane person is suited for urban city life, acting sophisticated and smooth.
Vacillate sounds like oscillating back and forth between two choices.
Think of vapor losing its flavor.
Venerate sounds like a veteran, whom we respect.
Veracity contains 'ver', like 'verify'.
Verbose has verbs and doses of extra words.
Vex rhymes with Rex, a dog that irritates the cat.
Think of a vile person who likes to fly around spreading nasty rumors.
Vindicate sounds like win dictate, meaning your proof wins the argument.
Virulent contains virus, reminding you of something harmful and toxic.
Think of viscous as viscous soup that flows as slow as us.
Vituperate sounds like viper hate, which is what harsh, biting insults feel like.
Volatile contains violet, and volatile liquids evaporate into thin air like vanishing ink.
Voracious sounds like ferocious, which describes a fierce, greedy desire for more.
Think of waves washing back and forth, unable to decide where to settle.
A wily person uses wiles to trick others.
Zealous people have an abundance of zeal.
Zenith starts with Z, the very top letter of our focus when reaching high.
Inside, an insidious plot hides its harm.
The word aberrant contains err, reminding you of behavior that errs from the standard path.
Anomaly comes from the Greek an- (not) and homalos (even or regular), meaning it does not follow the normal pattern.
Something banal has been heard so often that you feel like putting a ban on all of it.
Bene means well and -ficent comes from facere (to do), so a beneficent act is literally doing good.
Just as a bolster pillow props up your back, to bolster someone's case is to support and strengthen it.
A boorish person acts like a wild boar, charging around with crude and bad manners.
Cacophony comes from Greek roots kakos (bad) and phone (sound), making it a harsh noise.
Just as a skin callus becomes tough from friction, a callous person has an emotionally hardened heart.
A capricious person acts on a sudden caprice, shifting their mood or mind without any warning.
Commensurate shares a root with 'measure'; things that are commensurate have matching measures.
Think of a 'cornucopia', the horn of plenty, to remember that copious means abundant.
To debunk a rumor is to remove the 'bunk' or nonsense from it.
Aesthetic comes from the Greek aisthesis, "perception": it is about how things look and feel to the senses.
Ascetic comes from the Greek askesis, "exercise": an ascetic trains the body to do without comforts.
Castigate comes from the Latin castigare, "to correct or punish": to castigate is to correct someone with harsh words.
Caustic comes from the Greek kaustikos, "burning": caustic words burn like acid.
Precipitate comes from the Latin praeceps, "headlong": to precipitate an event is to send it rushing forward headfirst.
Prolific shares the Latin root proles, "offspring", with proliferate: both are about producing a lot.
Propensity comes from the Latin propensus, "leaning forward": a propensity is a leaning toward some kind of behavior.
Propitiate shares a root with propitious, "favorable": you propitiate people to make them favorable toward you.
Prosaic comes from prose, the ordinary language of everyday writing rather than poetry.
Reticent comes from the Latin reticere, "to keep silent", built on tacere, the same root as tacit.
Derivative work is derived from someone else's: it repeats rather than creates.
Catalyst comes from the Greek katalysis, "dissolving": a catalyst breaks a fixed situation apart so that change can happen.
Deride comes from Latin ridere, to laugh, the root of ridicule: to deride people is to laugh them down.
Desiccate comes from Latin siccus, dry: to desiccate something is to dry it out thoroughly.
Desultory comes from Latin desultor, a circus rider who leapt from horse to horse, just as desultory work jumps from one thing to another.
Diaphanous comes from Greek dia, through, and phainein, to show: a diaphanous veil lets the light show through it.
Diatribe comes from a Greek verb meaning to wear away, and a long diatribe wears down everyone who has to hear it.
Didactic comes from Greek didaskein, to teach: a didactic story is written to teach a lesson.
Diffident shares Latin fidere, to trust, with confident; the dif- (from dis-, not) marks a person who does not trust their own ability.
Dilatory comes from Latin dilatus, put off, a form of the verb that also gave English defer: a dilatory person keeps deferring.
Dirge comes from dirige, the opening Latin word of a chant in the church's service for the dead, which is why a dirge is a song of mourning.
Disabuse joins dis-, undo, with an old sense of abuse, to deceive: to disabuse someone is to undo a deception.
Discordant comes from Latin dis-, apart, and cor, heart: discordant views come from hearts set apart.
Discrepancy comes from Latin discrepare, to sound different: when two accounts do not sound the same, there is a discrepancy.
Impassive joins im-, not, to the Latin root of passion (pati, to suffer or feel): an impassive face shows no passion.
Reverent and revere share a Latin root, revereri, to stand in awe: a reverent person reveres what is before them.
Sagacious comes from Latin sagax, keen-scented, a word Romans used for good hunting dogs: a sagacious person sniffs out the truth.
Salubrious comes from Latin salus, health, also the root of salute: Romans greeted each other by wishing good health.
Abate comes from Old French abatre, to beat down: when a storm abates, its force is beaten down.
Abscond comes from Latin abscondere, to hide away: someone who absconds slips off and hides, often with the money.
Abstain comes from Latin abs-, away, and tenere, to hold: to abstain is to hold yourself away from something.
Admonish shares a Latin root with monitor: monere, to warn. To admonish someone is to warn them about their conduct.
Adulterate comes from Latin adulterare, to corrupt, a close relative of adultery: both spoil something that should stay pure.
Aggrandize contains grand, from Latin grandis, large: to aggrandize someone is to make them grander in power or in show.
Alacrity comes from Latin alacer, lively and eager, the same root as allegro, the music term for a quick, bright pace.
Disparage contains par, from the Latin for "equal": to disparage someone is to talk as if they are below par.
Disparate shares a Latin root, parare, with separate: disparate things are so unlike that they seem to belong in separate worlds.
Dissemble comes from the same Latin root as simulate: to dissemble is to simulate a feeling so the real one stays hidden.
Disseminate comes from the Latin for "seed," the root of seminal and seminar: to disseminate ideas is to scatter them like seed.
Dissonance comes from Latin dis-, "apart," and sonare, "to sound": ideas in dissonance sound wrong together, like clashing notes.
Distend shares the Latin tendere, "to stretch," with extend and tension: a distended belly is stretched out from inside.
Dogmatic comes from dogma, a belief that an authority says must not be questioned: a dogmatic person treats their own opinions that way.
Dubious shares its Latin root with doubt: a dubious claim is one you have good reason to doubt.
Ebullient comes from the Latin ebullire, "to boil over": an ebullient person bubbles over with joy.
Eclectic comes from the Greek eklegein, "to pick out": an eclectic person picks out the best from many sources.
Effrontery contains front, from the Latin frons, "forehead" or "face": effrontery is showing a bold face when you should feel shame.
Candor shares a root with candid and candle, Latin candere, to shine: candor lets the plain truth shine through.
Chicanery comes from the French chicaner, to quibble: it means winning by sly tricks and hair-splitting arguments rather than fair means.
Coagulate comes from Latin coagulum, rennet, the stuff cheesemakers use to curdle milk: to coagulate is to clot or curdle.
Coalesce comes from Latin co-, together, and alescere, to grow: separate parts grow together into one.
Cogent comes from Latin cogere, to drive together or compel: a cogent argument compels you to agree.
Complaisant comes from French complaire, to please: a complaisant person goes out of the way to please others. Do not confuse it with complacent, meaning smug.
Conciliatory comes from Latin conciliare, to bring together or win over, the root of reconcile: conciliatory words aim to reconcile.
Condone shares a root with donate, Latin donare, to give: when you condone a wrong, you give it a free pass.
Conflagration comes from Latin conflagrare, to burn up, from flagrare, to blaze: a conflagration is a blaze out of control.
Connoisseur comes from an old French word meaning to know, related to recognize: a connoisseur knows quality when they see or taste it.
Contrite comes from Latin contritus, ground down or crushed: a contrite person feels crushed by guilt over a wrong.
Conundrum ends in drum: a hard puzzle keeps drumming in your head until you work it out.
Convoluted comes from the Latin convolvere, 'to roll together': a convoluted story is rolled up in so many loops that it is hard to unwind.
Corroborate and robust share the Latin robur, 'strength': to corroborate a story is to make it stronger with evidence.
Credulous comes from the Latin credere, 'to believe', like credit and creed: a credulous person believes too easily.
Cursory comes from the Latin cursor, 'runner', like the cursor that races across a screen: a cursory look runs past the details.
Dearth is built from dear plus -th, like warmth from warm: when food is scarce, it grows dear, meaning costly.
Debacle comes from a French word for river ice breaking up: picture a frozen plan cracking apart all at once.
Decorum comes from the Latin decorus, 'fitting' or 'proper': decorum is behavior that fits the occasion.
Deference comes from defer, 'to yield': showing deference means you defer to someone else's wishes.
Deleterious begins with delete: something deleterious can wipe out your health bit by bit.
Elegy comes from the Greek elegos, a song of grief, and an elegy is still a poem that grieves for the dead.
Eloquent comes from the Latin e-, out, and loqui, to speak: an eloquent person speaks out with skill.
Embellish contains the French bel, beautiful (as in belle): to embellish a story is to make it prettier than the truth.
Empirical comes from the Greek empeiria, experience: empirical knowledge is learned by experience and testing, not by theory.
Emulate comes from the Latin aemulus, a rival: you emulate people when you try to match or even beat them.
Enervate comes from the Latin e-, out, and nervus, sinew: picture the sinews pulled out, leaving you limp. It is the opposite of energize.
Engender shares its Latin root with generate (generare, to beget): to engender trust or anger is to generate it.
Ephemeral comes from the Greek epi, on, and hemera, day: something ephemeral lasts about a day.
Epigram and telegram both end in gram, Greek for something written. Think of an epigram as a telegram of wit: short, because every word counts.
Equivocate joins the Latin aequus, equal, and vox, voice: words that speak with two equal voices, so no one can tell which meaning you intend.
Erudite comes from the Latin e-, out of, and rudis, rough or untaught (as in rude and rudimentary): an erudite person has been taught out of roughness.
Esoteric comes from the Greek eso, within: esoteric knowledge stays inside a small circle, while exoteric knowledge is for outsiders.
Assuage goes back to Latin suavis, sweet, the root of suave: to assuage a bitter feeling is to sweeten it.
Audacious comes from Latin audere, to dare (not audire, to hear): an audacious person dares to do what others will not.
Austere goes back to a Greek word for a dry, harsh taste; an austere room is dry in the same way, with nothing sweet or soft added.
Aver comes from Latin verus, true, the root of verify and veracity: to aver something is to declare it true.
Belie contains lie, and comes from an old English word for deceiving: a calm face that belies your nerves tells a lie about how you feel.
Bombastic comes from bombast, cotton stuffing once used to pad out clothes: bombastic speech is padded out with grand words.
Burgeon comes from an old French word for a bud: picture buds bursting open all over a tree in spring, and you have something that burgeons.
Buttress comes from an old French word meaning to push against: a stone buttress pushes back against a wall, and evidence can buttress an argument the same way.
Cajole rhymes with goal: you cajole someone with sweet talk until you reach your goal.
Alleviate comes from the Latin levis, meaning light, as in levity: to alleviate a pain is to make it lighter to carry.
Amalgamate comes from amalgam, the blend of mercury and other metals long used to fill teeth: to amalgamate is to blend things into one.
Ambiguous begins with the Latin ambi-, meaning both: an ambiguous remark can be taken both ways.
Ambivalent joins the Latin ambi-, 'both', with valere, 'to be strong': two opposite feelings pull with equal strength.
Ameliorate contains the Latin melior, meaning better: to ameliorate a bad situation is to make it better.
Anachronism contains the Greek chronos, 'time', as in chronology: an anachronism is something placed in the wrong time.
Analogous shares a root with analogy: when two things are analogous, you can explain one by drawing an analogy to the other.
Antipathy joins the Greek anti, 'against', and pathos, 'feeling': a feeling set firmly against someone or something.
Apathy is the Greek a-, 'without', plus pathos, 'feeling': apathy is a state without feeling or interest.
Appease has peace inside it, from the Old French pais, 'peace': you appease an angry person to restore the peace.
Arduous comes from the Latin arduus, 'steep': an arduous task feels like a long climb up a steep hill.
Articulate comes from the Latin articulus, 'small joint': to articulate a thought is to lay it out in clear, separate parts, like the segments of a finger.
Eulogy joins Greek eu (good) and logos (word): good words spoken about someone, usually at a funeral.
Euphemism comes from Greek eu (good) and pheme (speech): speaking of a bad thing in good-sounding words.
Evanescent comes from Latin evanescere, to vanish; the English word vanish grew from the same root.
Exacerbate shares a root with acerbic (Latin acerbus, bitter): to exacerbate a bad thing is to make it more bitter.
Exculpate is Latin ex (out of) plus culpa (blame), the root of culpable: it takes someone out of blame.
Exigent comes from Latin exigere, to demand, the same root as exact: an exigent problem demands action now.
Exonerate comes from Latin ex (off) and onus, oneris (a burden): to exonerate someone is to lift the burden of blame off them.
Expedient comes from Latin expedire, to free the feet: an expedient choice frees you to move toward what you want, right or not.
Expunge comes from Latin pungere, to prick, as in puncture: scribes pricked dots under a name to strike it from a list.
Extol comes from Latin extollere, to lift up: when you extol someone, you lift them up with praise.
Facetious comes from Latin facetia, a jest; it also holds all five vowels in order, a little joke built into the spelling.
Fallacious comes from Latin fallere, to deceive, the same root as false: a fallacious argument leads you to a false conclusion.
Officious comes from Latin officium, "duty", the root of office: an officious person treats every matter as their duty to manage.
Onerous comes from Latin onus, "burden", the same onus as in "the onus is on you".
Opaque comes from Latin opacus, "shaded": an opaque explanation leaves its meaning in the shade.
Opprobrium comes from Latin probrum, "a shameful act": opprobrium is the scorn heaped on someone who commits one.
Ostentatious comes from Latin ostentare, "to keep showing": an ostentatious person keeps showing off what they own.
Palliate comes from Latin pallium, "cloak": to palliate a fault is to throw a cloak over it so it looks less bad.
Panacea comes from Greek pan, "all", and akos, "cure": a panacea is a cure for all.
Paragon comes from Italian paragone, a touchstone used to test gold: a paragon is the standard others are tested against.
Parsimony comes from Latin parcere, "to spare": a person known for parsimony spares every coin.
Paucity comes from Latin paucus, "few": a paucity of anything means there are too few of them.
Pedantic comes from pedant, which came into English through French from Italian pedante, a schoolmaster: a pedantic person corrects everyone like a fussy teacher.
Penchant comes from French pencher, "to lean": a penchant is a natural leaning toward something.
Intractable comes from Latin tractare, to handle: an intractable problem is one nobody can get a handle on.
Intransigent comes via Spanish from Latin transigere, to settle a deal. Add in- (not) and you get someone who will not settle.
Inundate comes from Latin unda, a wave: to inundate is to send wave after wave over something.
Inveterate shares the Latin root veter-, old, with veteran: an inveterate habit is a veteran habit that has grown old with you.
Irascible and irate both come from Latin ira, anger: an irascible person turns irate at the smallest thing.
Itinerant shares the Latin root iter, a journey, with itinerary: an itinerant worker's whole life is an itinerary.
Laconic comes from Laconia, home of the Spartans, who were famous for short replies. To a king's threat beginning 'If I invade,' they answered only 'If.'
Lassitude comes from Latin lassus, weary: lassitude is a weariness so deep that it drains the will to act.
Laud comes from Latin laus, praise, as does laudable. Applaud has a different root, but it still helps: to laud someone is to applaud them with words.
Lethargic comes from Greek lethe, forgetfulness, the name of the river of forgetting in the Greek underworld: a lethargic person seems to have forgotten how to get moving.
Levity comes from Latin levis, light, the same root behind elevate and lever: levity is a light touch where weight is expected.
Loquacious comes from Latin loqui, to speak, also found in eloquent and soliloquy: a loquacious person speaks and speaks.
Lucid comes from Latin lucere, to shine: a lucid explanation lets light into a murky subject.
Luminous comes from Latin lumen, light, the same root as illuminate: something luminous gives off light.
Magnanimous joins Latin magnus, great, and animus, spirit: a great-spirited person rises above grudges.
Malinger comes from French malingre, sickly: a malingerer acts sickly to dodge work.
Malleable comes from Latin malleus, hammer: a malleable metal, or a malleable mind, can be hammered into a new shape.
Maudlin comes from Magdalene, once pronounced maudlin, because Mary Magdalene was often painted weeping.
Mendacious comes from Latin mendax, lying. Picture a mendacious person whose stories always need mending.
Mercurial comes from Mercury, the swift messenger god, and the metal named after him, which slides and splits apart unpredictably.
Meticulous comes from Latin metus, fear: a meticulous worker is almost afraid of making even one small mistake.
Mitigate comes from Latin mitis, mild: to mitigate damage is to make it milder.
Mollify comes from Latin mollis, soft: you mollify an angry person by softening their mood.
Morose comes from Latin morosus, peevish or hard to please: a morose person sulks and will not be cheered.
Impute shares a root with compute: Latin putare, 'to reckon'. To impute is to reckon a fault into someone's account.
Inchoate comes from Latin incohare, 'to begin': an inchoate plan has only just been started and has no shape yet.
Incipient comes from Latin incipere, 'to begin' (in- 'on' + capere 'to take'): something incipient is just taking hold.
Indigent comes from Latin indigere, 'to be in need': indigent people need help just to get by.
Indolent comes from Latin in- 'not' + dolere 'to feel pain': the indolent avoid the pain of hard work. Doctors still call a slow, painless tumor indolent.
Ineffable comes from Latin in- 'not' + effari 'to speak out': something ineffable cannot be spoken.
Inexorable comes from Latin in- 'not' + exorare 'to win over by pleading' (orare, 'to pray'): no prayer can stop it.
Ingenuous comes from Latin ingenuus, 'freeborn' and so 'frank'. Hear genuine inside it: an ingenuous person is genuine, with nothing hidden.
Inimical comes from Latin inimicus, 'enemy' (in- 'not' + amicus 'friend'): something inimical acts like an enemy.
Iniquity comes from Latin iniquus, 'unjust' (in- 'not' + aequus 'equal, fair'): iniquity treats people in a cruelly unfair way.
Innocuous comes from Latin in- 'not' + nocuus 'harmful', from nocere 'to harm' (as in noxious): innocuous things do no harm.
Insipid comes from Latin in- 'not' + sapidus 'tasty' (from sapere 'to taste', the root of savor): insipid things have no savor.
Insular comes from Latin insula, 'island' (as in peninsula): insular people live as if on an island, cut off from everyone else.
Hackneyed comes from the hackney, a horse kept for hire; ridden by everyone, it ended up worn out, like an overused phrase.
Harangue comes from Medieval Latin harenga, a speech given to a crowd. It also starts like harass, which is what a harangue does to its listeners.
Hedonist comes from Greek hedone, "pleasure": a hedonist lives to chase it.
Hegemony comes from Greek hegemon, "leader": a nation with hegemony leads and the rest follow.
Heresy comes from Greek hairesis, "a choosing": a heretic chooses a belief of his own over the official one.
Iconoclast joins Greek eikon, "image", and klastes, "breaker": first a smasher of holy images, now a smasher of sacred ideas.
Idolatry joins idol with Greek latreia, "worship": it is the worship of an idol.
Immutable holds Latin mutare, "to change", as in mutation; the im- means not, so it cannot change.
Impecunious holds Latin pecunia, "money", as in pecuniary; the im- means without, so it means without money.
Imperious comes from Latin imperium, "command", the root of empire: an imperious person gives orders like an emperor.
Impertinent is in- (not) plus pertinent, relevant: an impertinent remark was first one that did not belong, and the word came to mean cheeky.
Impervious comes from Latin per, "through", and via, "way"; with im- in front, nothing finds a way through.
Implacable shares Latin placare, "to calm", with placate and placid; im- means not, so it cannot be calmed.
Fatuous shares a root with infatuated, from Latin fatuus, 'foolish': people who are infatuated often say fatuous things.
Fervid comes from Latin fervere, 'to boil', the same root as fervent: fervid feelings are boiling hot.
Fickle sounds like flicker: a fickle heart flickers from one person to the next.
Flout rhymes with out: people who flout a rule step out of it in plain sight, as if daring anyone to stop them.
Foment comes from Latin fovere, 'to keep warm': to foment a revolt is to keep feeding its heat until it boils over.
Forestall comes from Old English foresteall, an ambush, literally a standing in front of someone on the road: to forestall something is to get in its way before it arrives.
Fortuitous comes from Latin fors, 'chance', the same root as fortune: a fortuitous event is left to chance.
Fractious shares a root with fracture, Latin frangere, 'to break': a fractious group keeps breaking the rules and breaking into quarrels.
Frugal comes from Latin frux, 'fruit' or 'produce': a frugal person makes every bit of the harvest last.
Garrulous comes from Latin garrire, 'to chatter': a garrulous seatmate chatters for the whole flight.
A goad was first a pointed stick for driving cattle; to goad someone is to keep poking at them until they move.
Gregarious comes from Latin grex, 'flock', also found in congregate: a gregarious person likes to be part of the flock.
Guile is the root of beguile: someone with guile can beguile you into trusting them.
Mundane comes from Latin mundus, world: mundane things belong to the ordinary everyday world.
Munificent comes from Latin munus, gift, and facere, to make: a munificent person makes many gifts.
Nadir comes from Arabic nazir, opposite: the nadir is the point opposite the zenith, the very bottom.
Nascent comes from Latin nasci, to be born, the root of natal and renaissance: a nascent thing has just been born.
Nebulous comes from Latin nebula, mist: a nebulous idea is misty, with no clear outline.
Nefarious comes from Latin nefas, a crime against divine law (ne-, not, plus fas, what is right).
Neophyte comes from Greek neos, new, and phytos, planted: a neophyte is newly planted in a field.
Obdurate comes from Latin obdurare, to harden, from durus, hard: an obdurate heart has hardened and will not bend.
Obfuscate comes from Latin fuscus, dark: to obfuscate is to darken a point until no one can see it clearly.
Obsequious comes from Latin obsequi, to comply, literally to follow after: an obsequious person follows the boss's every wish.
Obstinate comes from Latin obstinare, to persist, a relative of stare, to stand: the obstinate stand their ground and will not budge.
Obtuse comes from Latin obtusus, blunted: an obtuse mind is dull rather than sharp, like an angle too wide to come to a point.

reviews.checker_notes: Weakest points: plain uses 'light' twice in two senses ('So light and thin that light can shine'); try 'So thin and fine that you can see light through it.' Wrong answers: diachronic is too obscure to tempt most learners, and euphonious and cacophonous form an obvious sound-related pair a learner can set aside together; replace diachronic with sycophantic ('Flattering powerful people too much to win their favor.'), which shares -phan- and would tempt.

reviews.notes: Expanded the three-word definition, varied the examples beyond speeches by politicians, and replaced wrong answers with look-alikes (dialogue, dialect, tribulation, tribunal, diadem). reviews.notes: Expanded "Instructive (especially excessively)" into a full definition, changed "bossy" in the plain line to the lecturing sense, and sharpened the examples. It is shared stock phrasing, so 4; reword to 'Not the same as another thing in type or character.' Minor grammar: diffuse needs 'instead of being gathered'.

reviews.notes: Expanded "Wasting time" to cover both slowness and stalling tactics, rewrote vague examples, and replaced wrong answers with look-alikes (dilapidated, laudatory, dilute, predatory, dilettante). reviews.checker_notes: Weakest points: the definition follows Oxford's two senses in order ('slow to act' verbatim, 'intended to cause delay' reworded); short shared phrasing, but 'Inclined to put things off, or meant to stall for time.' would be safer. Hook is true (dilatus serves as the past participle of differre, source of defer) but hard to follow. 'poky' is childish slang; use 'procrastinating' or 'lax'.

reviews.notes: Kept the WordNet definition and the plain line. Rewrote examples to give clearer funeral clues and add a figurative use, replaced wrong answers with look-alikes (dredge, surge, serge, purge, dirk), used the true "dirige" origin for the hook, and swapped rare coronach for elegy.
reviews.checker_notes: Weakest points: the definition is WordNet's gloss word for word (allowed), but it is also Merriam-Webster's with one word changed ('grief' to 'mourning'), and it is long; a fresh version such as 'A slow, sad song or hymn performed to mourn someone who has died.' avoids both. dirk option rewords Merriam-Webster's 'a long straight-bladed dagger' and WordNet's gloss; acceptable. Plain: a tune is played, not sung; say 'song or piece of music played or sung'.

reviews.notes: Rewrote the parenthetical WordNet definition and the plain line (dropped "misconception"), fixed the "disabuse of the rumor" example, and replaced wrong answers, one of which was an antonym, with dis- look-alikes. reviews.notes: Split the senses cleanly: first sense is disagreement, other sense is clashing sound (the old one nearly copied the first). reviews.notes: Kept the WordNet definition, plain line and other sense. Plain repeats 'mismatch ... should match'; try 'A difference between two things that ought to agree.' desperation is a weak look-alike.

reviews.notes: Expanded the thin WordNet definition, rewrote the plain definition, and replaced the fragment example with a full sentence about a bridge. reviews.notes: Dropped the other sense, which named the word and repeated the first sense, and rewrote the examples so each gives a clue (the fragments are gone). reviews.checker_notes: Round 2: the massive option 'Of enormous size, weight or bulk.' matches no dictionary text I could find, so the copying issue is fixed. reviews.notes: Rewrote the plain definition so it no longer names the word, fixed the fragment and the ungrammatical "a reverent care" example, and replaced the made-up wrong answers with look-alikes. reviews.notes: Rewrote the plain definition so it no longer names the word, and replaced two weak examples with ones that give clear clues. The hook is true: Latin sagax meant keen-scented and was used of hunting dogs (from sagire, to perceive keenly). The overlapping other sense is gone. Weakest points: loquacious 'Fond of talking' is short phrasing that several dictionaries share. Plain 'so you make good choices' switches to 'you'. The definition is WordNet's terse text.

reviews.notes: Rewrote the thin definition and the plain definition (which named the word), replaced the duplicate other sense with the real "respectable place" sense, and swapped the fragment and redundant examples for ones with clear contrasts. Second review round 1: hook now credits the Latin greeting, not English salute, with the health meaning.
reviews.checker_notes: Round 2: the hook is now accurate. Salus is the root of salute, and Romans greeted each other by wishing health (salve, salutem). Weakest point: all four examples are about air, climate or a place, and two are about mountain air.

reviews.notes: Merged the two WordNet senses (make less intense, become less intense) into one definition, since they differ only in grammar, and added examples of the common "the storm abated" use. Rewrote the wrong answers, which copied Oxford, gave the hook the true Old French root, and replaced slake with common synonyms.
reviews.checker_notes: Weakest point: abrogate ('Officially cancel a law, treaty or agreement') sits near abate's legal sense (to end a nuisance or quash a writ), though that sense is not in the entry. Example 1 is close to the rubric's own model sentence.

reviews.notes: Replaced the two-word fragment example with a full sentence, and rewrote the wrong answers in my own words with their look-alikes (abhorrent, arrant, apparent, abrasive, abundant). Dropped the rare adjective deviate from the synonyms and added common ones.
reviews.checker_notes: Weakest point: examples 1 and 4 are both lab or medical settings, and example 1 is the generic 'technician noted' pattern the rubric warns about.

reviews.notes: Rewrote the WordNet definition to add the secrecy and escape that set the word apart from plain running away, and tightened the plain definition. reviews.checker_notes: Weakest point: examples 1 and 3 say nearly the same thing (a treasurer or accountant running off with money). Example 3 is WordNet's own example, extended, which is fine.

reviews.notes: Made the general meaning (going without a pleasure such as alcohol) the first sense, because it is the one learners meet most, and kept voting as an other sense in new words. Rewrote the examples to match, rewrote the -tain wrong answers that copied Oxford, and gave the hook its real Latin root.
reviews.checker_notes: Weakest point: attain ('Reach a goal') and obtain ('Come to have something') mean nearly the same, so a test-taker can rule both out together. Swap one for another -tain look-alike such as detain or contain.

reviews.notes: Made the reproving sense the first sense, since "advise" missed the scolding that the word carries, and kept the urging sense as one other sense in place of two near copies. Rewrote examples, plain definition and wrong answers to match, and replaced the noun reproof and the rare monish in the synonyms.
reviews.checker_notes: Weakest points: other sense 'Urge someone earnestly...' shares Oxford's short phrasing 'advise or urge (someone) earnestly' (not a whole-definition copy, so a note only). Wrong answers cherish, replenish and demolish share only the -ish ending, so they tempt little; replenish's 'Restore a supply to its full level' echoes Oxford's 'restore (a stock or supply) to a former level'.

reviews.notes: Shortened the long WordNet definition so the correct option no longer stands out by length, and replaced the fragment and the odd alchemist example. Rewrote the wrong answers in my own words with look-alikes, replaced the sound-alike "adult" hook with the true Latin root, and dropped the obscure synonyms load and stretch.
reviews.checker_notes: Weakest point: example 3 has a restaurant adulterating 'its honey', which is odd (a honey packer or supplier would be natural). Example 5 ('Laws exist to punish companies that adulterate food products') gives a weak cloze clue.

reviews.notes: WordNet gave only "add details to" (embellish), so I rewrote the definition for the test meaning: increase or exaggerate someone's power and importance. Rewrote examples, wrong answers and related words to fit that sense, and gave the hook the true root grandis.
reviews.checker_notes: Weakest point: the aggregate option 'Gather separate items into one mass or total.' echoes Merriam-Webster's 'to collect or gather into a mass or whole'. Several words differ, so a note only; rephrasing (for example 'Combine many separate figures into a single sum.') would remove the echo.

reviews.notes: Expanded the thin definition to show both speed and willingness, removed the repeated "cheerful" from the plain definition, and replaced the fragment and redundant examples. Rewrote the -acity wrong answers in my own words, replaced the nonsense hook with the true Latin root, and swapped smartness for common synonyms plus two antonyms.
reviews.checker_notes: Weakest point: the clarity option 'Clearness of thought or expression' is close to Random House's 'clearness of thought or style' (short shared phrasing, a note only).

reviews.notes: Expanded the thin WordNet definition and rewrote the plain one. Dropped the fragment example, added clue-giving ones, wrote five real look-alike wrong answers, explained the par root in the hook, and replaced "pick at" and "flatter" with closer related words.
reviews.checker_notes: No score under 4. Weakest point: the definition says 'scornfully', which is narrower than the word; disparaging talk is often mild and slighting rather than scornful. 'Speak of a person or thing as having little worth or importance' would cover both. Wrong answer for disengage is a reworded form of the WordNet gloss ('release from something that holds fast, connects, or entangles'), which Merriam-Webster shares word for word; WordNet is licensed and the text is reworded, so it is acceptable.

reviews.notes: Rewrote the definition in my own words (the WordNet text sat close to a Merriam-Webster sense) and fixed the overstated plain one. Dropped the near-copy other sense and the two fragment examples, added look-alike wrong answers, a hook with the real parare link to separate, and synonyms.
reviews.checker_notes: No score under 4. Definition follows the shape of Oxford's 'Essentially different in kind; not allowing comparison' (different in basic nature, hard to compare). It is reworded, not copied, so 4; a fresher version: 'So unlike one another that they share little and do not fit together easily.' Related: 'distinct' and 'diverse' fit less well than dissimilar and unlike; 'incongruous' or 'assorted' would be closer.

reviews.notes: Merged WordNet senses 1 and 2 into one clear definition about hiding real feelings, kept the distinct "behave affectedly" sense, and rewrote plain and examples to fit. Added look-alike wrong answers, a true simulate hook, and swapped sham and affect for dissimulate and disguise.
reviews.checker_notes: No score under 4. Weakest point: the wrong answer for resemble, 'Look or seem like another person or thing.', reuses the closing words of Oxford's resemble definition ('...; look or seem like'). It is a short common phrase, so 4; 'Be similar in looks or nature to someone or something else.' avoids it. The other sense 'Behave unnaturally or affectedly.' is WordNet text for a rare sense; harmless.

reviews.notes: The old hook was corrupted with stray symbols and markup; replaced it with the true seed root. Expanded the thin definition, rewrote the clumsy examples, added look-alike wrong answers, and dropped the spelling variants circularize and circularise.
reviews.checker_notes: No score under 4. Weakest point: eliminate and nominate share only the -minate ending, so they are weak look-alikes. germinate (shares -minate and the seed idea) or terminate would tempt more.

reviews.notes: Widened the definition to cover a clash between words and deeds, the use learners meet most, and replaced the two noise senses with one musical sense in my own words. Fixed the false hook, added look-alike wrong answers, and dropped noise and racket from the synonyms.
reviews.checker_notes: No score under 4. Definition tracks Oxford's figurative sense, 'A tension or clash resulting from the combination of two disharmonious or unsuitable elements' ('tense clash' between things that 'do not fit together'). Reworded, so 4; e.g. 'Conflict between things that ought to match but do not, such as...'. Examples: three of four use the same 'dissonance between X and Y' frame; recast one (e.g. a meeting full of dissonance). Wrong answers: sustenance, ordinance and provenance share only -nance; assonance and distance are the strong ones.

reviews.notes: "Become wider" missed the pressure from inside, so I rewrote the definition and dropped the two near-copy other senses. The examples wrongly tied it to heat; replaced them with belly, hose and vein cases. Added look-alike wrong answers, the true tendere hook, and more related words.
reviews.checker_notes: No score under 4. Definition is close to the stock wording shared by Oxford ('Swell or cause to swell by pressure from inside') and Cambridge ('swell and become large, especially because of pressure from inside'); reworded, so 4. Plain: 'because too much has been put inside' is inexact, since swelling usually comes from gas or fluid building up, not from something being put in; try 'To bulge and stretch because something inside is pushing outward.' Wrong answer for distill opens like Oxford's distil ('Purify (a liquid) by heating it...'); short and common, so 4.

reviews.notes: Added the refusal to hear other views to the definition and plain one, merged the two near-copy doctrine senses into one, and gave the examples clearer clues. The wrong answer for dramatic uses its theater sense, which is less tempting than the 'showy' sense, but it is accurate.

reviews.notes: Made the "questionable, not to be trusted" sense first, since the examples and test use lean that way, and kept the uncertain and unconvinced senses as other senses. Rewrote examples to fit one sense, replaced reused and lookalike-less wrong answers, fixed the misspelled hook, and matched related words to the new sense.
reviews.checker_notes: No score under 4. Sense 4: the other sense 'Uncertain in outcome; not at all sure to happen or succeed.' opens with Merriam-Webster's gloss for doubtful ('uncertain in outcome : undecided'), and Dictionary.com has 'of uncertain outcome' for dubious. Short shared phrasing, so 4; 'Not at all sure to happen or succeed.' on its own avoids it.

reviews.notes: Expanded the two-word WordNet definition, simplified the plain one, and gave the examples stronger and more varied clues. Added look-alike wrong answers, made the hook state the ebullire root plainly, and filled out synonyms and antonyms.
reviews.checker_notes: No score under 4. Weakest point: the emollient wrong answer, 'Making rough, dry skin feel soft and calm.', uses 'calm' oddly for skin; 'soft and soothed' reads better.

reviews.notes: Rewrote the definition and the plain one, which echoed Oxford and Merriam-Webster. Replaced the weak scholars example, added look-alike wrong answers, wrote a hook with the true Greek root, and replaced the wrong antonym "undiscriminating".
reviews.checker_notes: No score under 4. Related: the synonyms describe variety (diverse, varied, broad) but not the choosing idea, and 'broad' is vague. Drop 'broad'; 'assorted' or 'wide-ranging' alone is enough.

reviews.notes: Kept the WordNet definition and the hook. Rewrote the plain one, which was close to Oxford, replaced the fragment and the second medicine example, added look-alike wrong answers (efficiency is the classic confusion), and replaced rare related words.
reviews.checker_notes: No score under 4. Definition is WordNet's text (licensed), fine. Wrong answers: legacy and advocacy share only -acy; efficiency, effigy and fallacy are strong. 'It measures' is also slightly off, since efficacy is the power itself.

reviews.notes: Rewrote the awkward WordNet definition and the plain one, which used Merriam-Webster's "shameless boldness". Replaced two vague examples, added look-alike wrong answers, wrote a hook on the Latin frons that names the word, and replaced the off-sense synonym "assumption".

reviews.notes: Expanded the thin WordNet definition, reworded the plain line away from a dictionary's wording, and replaced the fragment example and two flat ones. reviews.notes: Made the placating meaning the first sense and kept the concessions sense as the other sense. reviews.notes: Kept the WordNet definition and the plain line, and added the figurative war sense as an other sense. Sharpened two examples, rewrote the wrong answers with labeled look-alikes (one copied Oxford), fixed the hook, which claimed the word contains "flagrant", and added synonyms.
